direct_claims: This chart compares countries by the share of people who are undernourished and the average daily supply of calories in 2023.
It belongs to the global food, nutrition, and development domain.
The publisher shown is Our World in Data.
The data source is the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.
The subtitle defines undernourishment here as the share of the total population with caloric intakes below minimum energy requirements.

The undernourishment measure is about intake falling below minimum energy requirements, so it captures chronic insufficiency in dietary energy rather than broader diet quality, micronutrient deficiency, or obesity.
The presence of regional labels in the legend indicates the chart is also meant to support cross-region comparison.
This chart matters because undernourishment is directly connected to hunger and inadequate energy intake in populations.
A note on the chart says values between 0% and 2.5% are shown as 2.5% on the chart.
This means some countries near the bottom of the plot may have different very low undernourishment values even if they appear aligned at the same level.
The chart includes labeled examples from multiple regions, along with regional coloring, which can help users compare both individual countries and broader geographic patterns.
derived_claims: The chart suggests a negative relationship: countries with lower calorie supply tend to have higher undernourishment, while countries with higher calorie supply tend to have lower undernourishment. — derived from overall inverse association in scatter positions.

Several labeled countries illustrate this pattern, including Haiti and DR Congo at high undernourishment with relatively low calorie supply, and Austria and Australia at low undernourishment with relatively high calorie supply. — derived from comparing labeled country positions on both axes.

The chart also shows that calorie supply alone does not perfectly determine undernourishment because countries with similar calorie supply can still have noticeably different undernourishment rates. — derived from vertical spread among points with similar x-values.

The clustering of many countries near low undernourishment at higher calorie supply levels is consistent with the idea that once basic food energy availability is sufficiently high, additional calories may be associated with smaller reductions in undernourishment than at very low supply levels. — derived from point clustering and flattening pattern.

Countries appearing in the upper-left portion of the chart face the combined challenge of low calorie availability and high undernourishment, which can indicate severe food insecurity. — derived from interpreting high y and low x positions using axis definitions.

The chart implies that raising food availability may help reduce undernourishment in many settings, but the dispersion across countries also suggests that distribution, conflict, poverty, and market access may influence outcomes. — derived from inverse association plus residual variation across countries.

Because the image does not provide the full dataset in tabular form, exact values for most unlabeled countries cannot be recovered with confidence from the chart alone. — derived from assessing limitations of reading precise values from image.

That means a country can have moderate or even high average calorie supply while still having undernourishment if food access is unequal, disrupted, or unaffordable for part of the population. — source: development economics and food security.

Governments, humanitarian agencies, and international organizations could use this kind of comparison to prioritize food assistance, agricultural support, and social protection. — source: public policy and humanitarian practice.
